title: Harsh Goenka Savours 10-Course Vegetarian Menu at World's No. 1 Restaurant Maido
excerpt: At Maido in Lima — No. 1 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — chef Mitsuharu Tsumura created his first-ever 10-course vegetarian tasting menu, and Goenka called it memorable.
body:
• RPG Group chairman Harsh Goenka dined at Maido in Lima, Peru — ranked No. 1 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — and tried its first-ever 10-course vegetarian menu.
  • Chef Mitsuharu "Micha" Tsumura built the tasting menu around Nikkei cuisine — Japanese techniques fused with Peruvian ingredients — using Amazonian nuts, squash, cassava, seitan, wakame, heart of palm, mashua and rocoto.
  • Goenka called it "a memorable meal" and praised the menu as "flavourful, inventive and delicious" in an X post that drew wide reactions from Indian food lovers.
  • The vegetarian tasting at a Japanese-Peruvian restaurant shows how seriously the world's top kitchens now take plant-based dining.

Ten vegetarian courses in Lima

Harsh Goenka's latest meal has the Indian internet talking. The RPG Group chairman shared pictures on X from Maido in Lima, Peru — the restaurant that topped the World's 50 Best Restaurants list in 2025 — where chef Mitsuharu "Micha" Tsumura created his first-ever 10-course vegetarian menu.

"A memorable meal at Maido, Lima, Peru, the world's No. 1 restaurant, where Japanese techniques meet Peruvian influences in Nikkei cuisine," Goenka wrote, alongside photographs of the dishes and one with Tsumura himself. "Chef Mitsuharu Tsumura created his first-ever 10-course vegetarian menu — flavourful, inventive and delicious. A truly special experience."

Context & Background

Maido opened in October 2009 in Lima's Miraflores district and has become the defining restaurant of Nikkei cuisine — the fusion of Japanese technique with Peruvian ingredients and flavours that grew out of generations of Japanese immigration to Peru. Its No. 1 ranking on the 2025 World's 50 Best list cemented Lima's place at the top of global fine dining.

What makes Goenka's meal notable is that the vegetarian menu was not a set of vegetable versions of Maido's regular dishes. Tsumura built it deliberately around the restaurant's Japanese-Peruvian identity, without meat or seafood, using ingredients such as Amazonian nuts, squash, cassava, seitan, wakame, heart of palm, mashua, rocoto and yellow chilli across the ten courses.

Impact & Analysis

Reactions on X ranged from surprise to humour. "In Peru and a Japanese restaurant serving 10-course vegetarian food!! Simply wow," one commenter wrote. Another joked: "Ten vegetarian courses in Peru. Meanwhile, Paneer would like to know why it's been doing all the overtime back home." One user suggested a South Indian-Thai vegetarian tasting menu in the same spirit, while others read the meal as a sign of the times: "Great to see the world showing interest in vegetarianism."

The subtext is hard to miss. When the world's best restaurant builds its first-ever vegetarian tasting menu, it confirms what Indian diners have long known: vegetarian food, done with intent, needs no apology. The world's elite kitchens are catching up to a tradition India has practiced for millennia — and an Indian billionaire's endorsement gives that story legs.

Diaspora Angle

Goenka's meal lands in the sweet spot of diaspora food culture: Indian vegetarians abroad have spent decades navigating menus that treated them as an afterthought, while Peruvians of Japanese descent built a cuisine that treats fusion as identity. That an Indian industrialist celebrated a vegetarian menu in Lima — a city whose food culture is itself a product of Asian diaspora — makes this a quiet landmark for the global Indian palate.

What's Next

Maido's vegetarian tasting may be a one-off experiment or the start of a permanent menu — either way, it signals where fine dining is heading. For India's own restaurants, which have struggled to convert the country's vegetarian depth into global fine-dining currency, the lesson is on the plate: heritage ingredients, treated with ambition.
